## Front end: it wasn't a step at all

Stage 4 deployed *"the app"* while **nothing in any stage created it**. The front end existed purely as an assumption. Now:

**Stage 4 — The application, and the pipeline that ships it**
- Next.js project: routing, layout, API client, `/health` for the target group
- Operator shell: customer switcher, run list from RDS, asset view that renders **whatever exists**
- Server-side: intake and ACK endpoints, `/api/*` configured for POST through CloudFront
- *Then* both pipelines

**Why together:** the pipeline has nothing to ship until the app exists, so building them in one stage makes the first deploy the first test of the pipeline.

Plus a **front-end-by-stage table**, since it's genuinely a thread rather than one stage — shell at 4, ingest at 5, asset view filling in at 6, run state at 8, chat at 9, deploy at 10. What appears when is now traceable instead of implied.

## To answer directly: it's a *new* sandbox

You're right that the generation box doesn't exist by stage 10 — it died when that run's `finish_run` landed. **A deploy is its own run, so it spins its own fresh box.**

What that box hydrates is different too: **the finished artifacts from `rev-<n>/`**, not a brain. Generation reads a brain and produces outputs; deploy reads those outputs and pushes them. Same tree, opposite direction.

Playwright is in the sandbox because the brief requires it:

> The browser runs where the agent runs. Not on your machine — that breaks the entire paradigm.

And it's already baked into the template for HTML→PNG rendering, so deploy needs **no new dependency and no second template**. Only three things differ from a generation run: the credentials, the allowed tools, and the prompt.

## Two wording defects, both mine

**Stage 10 said "Playwright in the sandbox" without saying *which* sandbox.** My trimming pass dropped that, which is exactly what prompted your question.

**Worse — the Deploy section opened with "same box shape, same files."** "Shape" was the intended word, but "same box" invites precisely the wrong reading, and "same files" was just wrong: deploy reads outputs where generation reads a brain. Now:

> The same *shape* of event as everything else — a clean box, the right files in, a prompt — plus a browser, credentials, and a different instruction. **Not the same box: that one is long dead.** A deploy is its own run and gets its own.

The detailed reference section already had it right (*"Every deploy is still its own run in its own fresh box"*), so this was a summary that had drifted from the thing it summarised — the same failure mode as the duplicated Terraform and stack sections. Worth me watching for on the next trim.

- **`comment` → `message`** in the round-trip criterion.

just had my meeting and we do not need to deploy the frontend so we can host locally, just the sandbox needs to not be local. If we use Supabase instead how much easier would the implementation be? We can locally run the frontend and backend.

--- ASSISTANT [2026-08-10 14:32:03] ---
That's a significant simplification, and it removes the riskiest hours — the ones that earn no points. Let me quantify it honestly.

## Compliance first: local backend is fine

Checking each disqualifier, because this is the kind of change that quietly breaks one:

- *"The backend launching the agent as a subprocess on its own box"* — backend on your laptop, agent in E2B. **Different machines.** ✓
- *"Any agent run on your laptop"* — still never. Only the *backend* moves local. ✓
- Everything else (work out of the box, box identity, ordering, third brand) is indifferent to where the backend runs. ✓

One thing gets *harder*, not easier: with the backend local, the temptation to spawn the agent next to it goes up, and there's no IAM to lean on any more. So the lint rule, the missing agent SDK dependency, and the DB constraint requiring a `sandbox_id` become the whole enforcement story rather than a supporting one.

## The problem local backend creates — and why Supabase solves it

If the API is on `localhost`, **the sandbox can't reach it.** Our ACK path was `sandbox → CloudFront → ALB → EC2`. That's gone, and the alternatives are a tunnel (ngrok/cloudflared — a fragile moving part in a demo) or something else.

Supabase makes it a non-problem: **the agent writes to Supabase directly and never calls our backend at all.**

```
backend (laptop) ──outbound──▶ E2B: create box, write HYDRATION.md
agent (E2B) ─────────────────▶ Supabase Storage: upload artifacts
agent (E2B) ─────────────────▶ Supabase Postgres: insert rows
backend (laptop) ──outbound──▶ Supabase: read everything back
```

**No inbound connection to your laptop, ever.** Everything is outbound. That's what makes local hosting actually work rather than work-with-a-tunnel.

## What disappears

| Deleted | |
|---|---|
| VPC, subnets, NAT, IGW, route tables | ~a third of the Terraform |
| VPC endpoints (S3, SSM×3, Secrets Manager, STS, Logs) | all of them |
| Internal ALB + CloudFront + VPC origin + cache behaviours | the entire edge |
| EC2 + instance profile + SSM agent | the whole compute layer |
| ECR + image build + SSM Run Command pipeline | the app pipeline |
| tfstate bucket + native locking + OIDC role | the bootstrap stage |
| Secrets Manager + STS AssumeRole + session policies | replaced by RLS |
| Terraform | replaced by SQL migrations |

**Stages 2 and 3 vanish. Stage 4 loses its pipeline half.** And 5 of the 11 functional checks evaporate, because every one of them was infrastructure plumbing: SSM endpoints, CloudFront POST, ALB 502s, Terraform locking, OIDC trust scope.

Estimate: **most of a day**, and it's the day with the highest chance of eating into stage 10 — which is the auto-DQ.

## The one genuinely better design

STS session policies get replaced by **RLS**, and it's an upgrade for this trial specifically.

The backend mints a short-lived JWT carrying a `revision_id` claim, hands it to the sandbox, and RLS policies on both `storage.objects` and the artifact tables restrict every write to that revision's prefix. Tenant isolation becomes **enforced by the database where the data lives**, not by a credential scope wrapped around it.

That's a stronger answer to the leak test than the AWS version was — and it means the "credentials cannot read another revision's prefix" test in stage 7 becomes a SQL-level assertion, which is much easier to write and much harder to fake.

The ACK endpoint also disappears: constraints and RLS become the rejecting authority, and Postgres returns the error text straight to the agent. Loud failure, one place, no custom endpoint to keep honest.

## What we lose

- **The AWS build**, which was your earlier call. Nothing compliance-relevant goes with it, and the interviewer said outright he doesn't care where it's deployed.
- **"Everything in the VPC"** becomes moot rather than violated — there's no VPC.
- Terraform as an IaC demonstration, partly replaced by versioned SQL migrations.

## My recommendation

**Take it.** Supabase Postgres + Storage, `next dev` locally, E2B for sandboxes, RLS for isolation. The queue stays the `runs` table with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` — that's unchanged and works identically.

Two things I'd want to confirm before rewriting the roadmap:

1. **Hosted Supabase or local `supabase start`?** Hosted, I'd say — the sandbox needs to reach it, and a local Supabase has the same unreachability problem as a local API.
2. **Does "runs locally" mean a reviewer clones and runs it?** If so, hosted Supabase plus `.env` makes that a two-command setup, which is a better answer to *"it should run"* than an AWS account they don't have access to.

Say go and I'll rewrite the stack table, the architecture diagram, and stages 2–7. It's a big edit but it's mostly deletion.

## The new shape

```
   every connection is OUTBOUND — nothing connects in to your machine

   YOUR MACHINE (localhost)            E2B  ── the only remote piece
   Next.js: React + API      ──▶       Sandbox, one per run
   never runs an agent                 opaque run id + scoped JWT
        │                                   │
        │ read + reconcile                  │ upload artifacts, insert rows
        │ mint run JWT                      │ never speaks to the backend
        ▼                                   ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  SUPABASE (hosted)                               │
   │  Postgres — runs table IS the queue              │
   │  Storage  — brains/<kit>/…  work/<task>/rev-<n>/ │
   │  RLS on every table, deny by default             │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## What made local hosting actually work

A sandbox can't reach `localhost` — so the ACK path was the blocker. Supabase removes the need for one entirely: **the agent writes to Storage and Postgres directly and never speaks to the backend.** Every connection is outbound. No tunnel, nothing to expose.

That also deletes the ACK endpoint. The **database** accepts or rejects — a policy, a `NOT NULL`, a uniqueness constraint — and Postgres returns the error text straight to the agent. Loud failure, one place, no endpoint of ours to keep honest.

## Isolation got better, not just simpler

RLS replaces STS. A short-lived run JWT carries `revision_id` and `brand_kit_id`; policies make those the only rows and objects the run can touch.

**The cross-tenant leak is now a database rule.** An Emplifi run carries an Emplifi `brand_kit_id`, so the mis-tagged `partner-lockup.svg` row is simply *not visible to it*. That turns the leak test into a SQL assertion — far harder to fake than a green tick, and enforced where the data lives rather than wrapped around it.

## One new sharp edge, with its own check

**`service_role` bypasses RLS completely.** Every guarantee rests on it never entering a sandbox environment, so it's check #2 with a hard failure — the launch payload is scanned before a box is created. Not a footnote.

## What went, and what it cost

Deleted: VPC · subnets · NAT · endpoints · ALB · CloudFront · EC2 · ECR · SSM pipeline · Terraform · tfstate · OIDC · Secrets Manager · STS. **Two stages vanish, a third loses half its work**, and 5 of 11 functional checks evaporated — all infrastructure plumbing. Four RLS checks replaced them.

**Two honest regressions I recorded rather than buried:**

1. Independent digest verification moves from **synchronous** (an endpoint checked before writing the row) to **reconciliation-time**. The agent still self-verifies in-run, so immediate feedback stays — the *independent* check lands seconds later.
2. "The backend can't call the image model" is now **discipline, not a wall** — it holds the keys in order to pass them in. Guards 1 and 2 (no SDK dependency, `sandbox_id` constraint) do the actual enforcing.

Also added `pg_cron` for soft-delete cleanup, since Storage has no lifecycle rules — the old S3 plan doesn't carry over.

**`.env.example` rewritten** with the Supabase block and that warning on `service_role`. Your `.env` is untouched and still gitignored.

Gate 0 is unchanged and still next — it never needed any of this.

## The strongest evidence

**The eval layer needed zero changes.** 144 tests, all passing, not one line touched. The grep above returns only substring matches inside `existsSync` — no S3, no STS, no AWS anywhere in it. And `validateRunsSchema` still asserts exactly the right things: `runs.sandbox_id NOT NULL`, `artifacts.storage_key NOT NULL`. Both remain correct on Supabase Postgres.

That's not luck — it means the checks were written against the *properties* rather than the provider. If quality had actually depended on AWS, this rewrite would have broken tests.

## Constraint by constraint

| Disqualifier | Before → After |
|---|---|
| Only the agent moves work out | ✓ → **stronger**. No ACK endpoint at all now; the backend isn't even in the path |
| No tenant in box identity | ✓ → ✓ *(one nuance, below)* |
| Backend not co-located with agent | ✓ → ✓, **weaker enforcement** *(recorded)* |
| No agent on a laptop | ✓ → ✓ unchanged. E2B only |
| No work only on a box | ✓ → ✓ unchanged |
| No hardcoded ordering | ✓ → ✓ unchanged. Same runs table, same `SKIP LOCKED` |
| Third brand, zero code | ✓ → **stronger**. RLS filters by kit generically, so a new brand needs no policy change |

**Every SKILL.md invariant is untouched** — plate-first, one plate per size, live HTML, logo proportions, `DESIGN.md` wins, inspirations advisory, never publish. None of them ever touched infrastructure. Gate 0 is byte-for-byte the same work.

## What genuinely improved

Cross-tenant isolation moved from a credential wrapper into the database, so the leak test is now a SQL assertion. No inbound surface exists at all. No ACK endpoint of ours to keep honest. A reviewer can actually run the thing — a better answer to *"it should run"* than a cloud account they can't access. And two stages left the schedule from exactly the place that threatened the auto-DQ stage.

## What genuinely got worse — both already in the doc

1. **Independent digest verification** moved from synchronous to reconciliation-time. The agent still self-verifies in-run, so loud failure survives; the *independent* check lands seconds later.
2. **"The backend can't call the image model"** went from a wall to a discipline, since it holds the keys to pass them in. Guards 1 and 2 do the enforcing.

## The nuance I found

The run JWT carries `brand_kit_id` as a claim. That's still compliant — identity means template, name and tags, not a runtime payload, and the hydration file already names the kit. But it's the **one place the new design puts a tenant string into a credential**, where the old STS policy named only an opaque path prefix.

**It's avoidable.** Carry only `revision_id`, and let the policy derive the kit by joining `revisions → requests`:

```sql
kit_id = (select brand_kit_id from requests q
          join revisions r on r.request_id = q.id
          where r.id = (auth.jwt() ->> 'revision_id')::uuid)
```

Same filtering, same guarantee — and then **no credential anywhere names a tenant.** It also makes the claim un-forgeable in a useful way: you can't widen your access by editing a kit id, because the kit isn't yours to state.

Small change, strictly tighter. Want me to make it?

--- ASSISTANT [2026-08-10 14:59:00] ---
Two findings, and one is a **long-lead blocker you should start right now**.

## ⚠️ Organization verification is mandatory — start this first

gpt-image-2 is gated behind OpenAI's **organization verification**, and this is *independent of usage tier* — even Tier 5 accounts must complete it separately. Without it, every call 403s no matter how the key is configured.

What it needs:

- A **physical government-issued ID** (passport or driver's licence) from a supported country
- A **live selfie / liveness check** — handled by Persona
- Your organisation's legal name, registered address, and possibly a tax or business registration number

**Timeline: minutes to 24 hours, occasionally days.** And the constraint that bites: **one ID can verify only one organisation every 90 days.** So if the card's org is already verified under someone else's ID, or you verify the wrong org, you're locked out for three months.

Do this before anything else — it's the only item with a queue.

## The key attribute that actually matters

When you create the key, set:

> **Model capabilities → Write** *(shown as "Request" in some views)*

That single permission is what OpenAI's RBAC docs describe as *"Make requests to chat completions, audio, embeddings, and images"* — images included. It's what produces the `model.request` scope.

**The failure mode to avoid:** a restricted key with only Chat Completions enabled returns `401 — Missing scopes: model.request`. Several people have hit exactly this, because the `model.request` scope only appears in the UI once Model capabilities is set to Request. A read-only key won't work either.

Two things I'd also do:

- **Make it a project key, not a user key** — revocable and attributable without touching your account
- **Set a project spend limit.** Gate 0 is roughly 60–80 image calls; a cap means a bug can't quietly run up the company card

## Then

Paste it into `.env` line 7:

```
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-...
```

Already gitignored — verified earlier with `git check-ignore`.

## One thing I'd like to add before you spend anything

A **preflight script** that calls `GET /v1/models/gpt-image-2` — which is **free**, no image generated. It tells us three things apart:

- Key invalid → `401`
- Key valid but wrong scope → `401 Missing scopes: model.request`
- Key and scope fine but org unverified → `403`
- All good → `200`

Worth having because otherwise the first failure looks identical to a bug in my plate code, and we'd waste time in the wrong place. Roughly 20 lines in `eval/scripts/`. Want me to write it?

Sources: [API organization verification](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10910291-api-organization-verification) · [RBAC / key permissions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/rbac) · [Assign API key permissions](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8867743-assign-api-key-permissions) · [gpt-image-2 verification requirement](https://help.apiyi.com/en/gpt-image-2-api-organization-verified-error-fix-en.html) · [`model.request` scope in the UI](https://community.openai.com/t/api-key-permissions-ui-model-request-scope-only-appears-when-model-capabilities-is-set-to-request/1374480)

Confirmed — here's the exact path.

## Where to click

**→ [platform.openai.com/settings/organization/general](https://platform.openai.com/settings/organization/general)**

Or navigate manually:

```
platform.openai.com
  └─ Settings  (gear icon, top right)
       └─ Organization
            └─ General          ← the "Verify Organization" button is here
```

Click **Verify Organization**. That hands you off to Persona for the ID and liveness check.

## Before you click

Two things worth getting right first, because of the 90-day lock:

**1. Confirm you're in the right organisation.** If the account has more than one, the org switcher is top-left. Verification attaches to the org you're *currently in* — and since one ID can only verify one org every 90 days, verifying the wrong one costs you three months.

**2. Have the details matching official records.** Legal name exactly as registered, current registered or operating address. Mismatches are the most common cause of "Organization could not be verified."

## What you'll need in hand

- Physical government-issued ID — passport or driver's licence
- A device that can photograph it, plus take a selfie for the liveness check
- The org's legal name and registered address

## After it succeeds

Access takes **up to 15 minutes to propagate**, so an immediate 403 right after verifying isn't necessarily a failure — wait and retry before debugging anything.

Then create the key at **[platform.openai.com/settings/organization/api-keys](https://platform.openai.com/settings/organization/api-keys)** with **Model capabilities → Write**, scoped to a project, with a spend limit.

---

While that's in the queue, say the word on the **preflight script** — `GET /v1/models/gpt-image-2`, free, no image generated. It distinguishes *key invalid* / *wrong scope* / *org unverified* / *all good* in one command, so when you paste the key we know instantly whether the setup is done rather than guessing from a failure inside my plate code.

okay ill read the documentation, meanwhile read what I found about the response api and the other one that helps iterate on an image. this sounds familiar to the phase where the user can itereate on a created asset: Overview

The OpenAI API lets you generate and edit images from text prompts using GPT Image models, including our latest, gpt-image-2. You can access image generation capabilities through two APIs:

Image API

Starting with gpt-image-1 and later models, the Image API provides two endpoints, each with distinct capabilities:

Generations: Generate images from scratch based on a text prompt
Edits: Modify existing images using a new prompt, either partially or entirely
Responses API

The Responses API allows you to generate images as part of conversations or multi-step flows. It supports image generation as a built-in tool, and accepts image inputs and outputs within context.

Compared to the Image API, it adds:

Multi-turn editing: Iteratively make high fidelity edits to images with prompting
Flexible inputs: Accept image File IDs as input images, not just bytes
The Responses API image generation tool uses its own GPT Image model selection. For details on mainline models that support calling this tool, refer to the supported models below.

Choosing the right API

If you only need to generate or edit a single image from one prompt, the Image API is your best choice.
If you want to build conversational, editable image experiences with GPT Image, go with the Responses API.
With the Image API, you choose a GPT Image model directly. With the Responses API, you choose a mainline model that supports the image generation tool; the tool handles GPT Image model selection. Responses API requests include the mainline model’s token usage in addition to image generation costs.

Both APIs let you customize output by adjusting quality, size, format, and compression. Transparent backgrounds depend on model support.

This guide focuses on GPT Image.

To ensure these models are used responsibly, you may need to complete the API Organization Verification from your developer console before using GPT Image models, including gpt-image-2, gpt-image-1.5, gpt-image-1, and gpt-image-1-mini.

A beige coffee mug on a wooden table
Generate Images

You can use the image generation endpoint to create images based on text prompts, or the image generation tool in the Responses API to generate images as part of a conversation.

To learn more about customizing the output (size, quality, format, compression), refer to the customize image output section below.

You can set the n parameter to generate multiple images at once in a single request (by default, the API returns a single image).

Image API
Responses API
Generate an image
from openai import OpenAI
import base64

client = OpenAI()

response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-5.6",
    input="Generate an image of gray tabby cat hugging an otter with an orange scarf",
    tools=[{"type": "image_generation"}],
)

# Save the image to a file
image_data = [
    output.result
    for output in response.output
    if output.type == "image_generation_call"
]

if image_data:
    image_base64 = image_data[0]
    with open("otter.png", "wb") as f:
        f.write(base64.b64decode(image_base64))
Multi-turn image generation

With the Responses API, you can build multi-turn conversations involving image generation either by providing image generation calls outputs within context (you can also just use the image ID), or by using the previous_response_id parameter. This lets you iterate on images across multiple turns—refining prompts, applying new instructions, and evolving the visual output as the conversation progresses.

With the Responses API image generation tool, supported tool models can choose whether to generate a new image or edit one already in the conversation. The optional action parameter controls this behavior: keep action: "auto" to let the model decide, set action: "generate" to always create a new image, or set action: "edit" to force editing when an image is in context.

Force image creation with action
from openai import OpenAI
import base64

client = OpenAI()

response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-5.6",
    input="Generate an image of gray tabby cat hugging an otter with an orange scarf",
    tools=[{"type": "image_generation", "action": "generate"}],
)

# Save the image to a file
image_data = [
    output.result
    for output in response.output
    if output.type == "image_generation_call"
]

if image_data:
    image_base64 = image_data[0]
    with open("otter.png", "wb") as f:
        f.write(base64.b64decode(image_base64))
If you force edit without providing an image in context, the call will return an error. Leave action at auto to have the model decide when to generate or edit.

Streaming

The Responses API and Image API support streaming image generation. You can stream partial images as the APIs generate them, providing a more interactive experience.

You can adjust the partial_images parameter to receive 0-3 partial images.

If you set partial_images to 0, you will only receive the final image.
For values larger than zero, you may not receive the full number of partial images you requested if the full image is generated more quickly.
Responses API
Image API
Stream an image
from openai import OpenAI
import base64

client = OpenAI()


def save_base64_image(filename, image_base64):
    image_bytes = base64.b64decode(image_base64)
    with open(filename, "wb") as f:
        f.write(image_bytes)


stream = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-5.6",
    input="Draw a gorgeous image of a river made of white owl feathers, snaking its way through a serene winter landscape",
    stream=True,
    tools=[{"type": "image_generation", "partial_images": 2}],
)

for event in stream:
    if event.type == "response.image_generation_call.partial_image":
        idx = event.partial_image_index
        save_base64_image(f"river-partial-{idx}.png", event.partial_image_b64)
    elif event.type == "response.completed":
        image_data = [
            output.result
            for output in event.response.output
            if output.type == "image_generation_call"
        ]

        if image_data:
            save_base64_image("river-final.png", image_data[0])

from openai import OpenAI
import base64

client = OpenAI()


def encode_image(file_path):
    with open(file_path, "rb") as image_file:
        return base64.b64encode(image_file.read()).decode("utf-8")


def create_file(file_path):
    with open(file_path, "rb") as file_content:
        result = client.files.create(file=file_content, purpose="vision")
    return result.id


prompt = """Generate a photorealistic image of a gift basket on a white background
labeled 'Relax & Unwind' with a ribbon and handwriting-like font,
containing all the items in the reference pictures."""

base64_image1 = encode_image("body-lotion.png")
base64_image2 = encode_image("soap.png")
file_id1 = create_file("bath-bomb.png")
file_id2 = create_file("incense-kit.png")

response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-5.6",
    input=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "input_text", "text": prompt},
                {
                    "type": "input_image",
                    "image_url": f"data:image/png;base64,{base64_image1}",
                },
                {
                    "type": "input_image",
                    "image_url": f"data:image/png;base64,{base64_image2}",
                },
                {
                    "type": "input_image",
                    "file_id": file_id1,
                },
                {
                    "type": "input_image",
                    "file_id": file_id2,
                },
            ],
        }
    ],
    tools=[{"type": "image_generation"}],
)

image_generation_calls = [
    output for output in response.output if output.type == "image_generation_call"
]

image_data = [output.result for output in image_generation_calls]

if image_data:
    image_base64 = image_data[0]
    with open("gift-basket.png", "wb") as f:
        f.write(base64.b64decode(image_base64))
else:
    print(response.output_text)
Edit an image using a mask

You can provide a mask to indicate which part of the image should be edited.

When using a mask with GPT Image, additional instructions are sent to the model to help guide the editing process accordingly.

Masking with GPT Image is entirely prompt-based. The model uses the mask as guidance, but may not follow its exact shape with complete precision.

If you provide multiple input images, the mask will be applied to the first image.

Responses API

Mask requirements

The image to edit and mask must be of the same format and size (less than 50MB in size).

The mask image must also contain an alpha channel. If you’re using an image editing tool to create the mask, make sure to save the mask with an alpha channel.

You can modify a black and white image programmatically to add an alpha channel.

Add an alpha channel to a black and white mask
from PIL import Image
from io import BytesIO

# 1. Load your black & white mask as a grayscale image
mask = Image.open("mask.png").convert("L")

# 2. Convert it to RGBA so it has space for an alpha channel
mask_rgba = mask.convert("RGBA")

# 3. Then use the mask itself to fill that alpha channel
mask_rgba.putalpha(mask)

# 4. Convert the mask into bytes
buf = BytesIO()
mask_rgba.save(buf, format="PNG")
mask_bytes = buf.getvalue()

# 5. Save the resulting file
img_path_mask_alpha = "mask_alpha.png"
with open(img_path_mask_alpha, "wb") as f:
    f.write(mask_bytes)
Image input fidelity

The input_fidelity parameter controls how strongly a model preserves details from input images during edits and reference-image workflows. For gpt-image-2, omit this parameter; the API doesn’t allow changing it because the model processes every image input at high fidelity automatically.

Because gpt-image-2 always processes image inputs at high fidelity, image input tokens can be higher for edit requests that include reference images. To understand the cost implications, refer to the vision costs section.

Customize Image Output

You can configure the following output options:

Size: Image dimensions (for example, 1024x1024, 1024x1536)
Quality: Rendering quality (for example, low, medium, high)
Format: File output format
Compression: Compression level (0-100%) for JPEG and WebP formats
Background: Opaque or automatic
size, quality, and background support the auto option, where the model will automatically select the best option based on the prompt.

gpt-image-2 doesn’t currently support transparent backgrounds. Requests with background: "transparent" aren’t supported for this model.

Size and quality options

gpt-image-2 accepts any resolution in the size parameter when it satisfies the constraints below. Square images are typically fastest to generate.

Popular sizes	
1024x1024 (square)

1536x1024 (landscape)

1024x1536 (portrait)

2048x2048 (2K square)

2048x1152 (2K landscape)

3840x2160 (4K landscape)

2160x3840 (4K portrait)

auto (default)

Size constraints	
Maximum edge length must be less than or equal to 3840px

Both edges must be multiples of 16px

Long edge to short edge ratio must not exceed 3:1

Total pixels must be at least 655,360 and no more than 8,294,400

Quality options	
low
medium
high
auto (default)

Use quality: "low" for fast drafts, thumbnails, and quick iterations. It is the fastest option and works well for many common use cases before you move to medium or high for final assets.

Outputs that contain more than 2560x1440 (3,686,400) total pixels, typically referred to as 2K, are considered experimental.

Output format

The Image API returns base64-encoded image data. The default format is png, but you can also request jpeg or webp.

If using jpeg or webp, you can also specify the output_compression parameter to control the compression level (0-100%). For example, output_compression=50 will compress the image by 50%.

Using jpeg is faster than png, so you should prioritize this format if latency is a concern.

Limitations

GPT Image models (gpt-image-2, gpt-image-1.5, gpt-image-1, and gpt-image-1-mini) are powerful and versatile image generation models, but they still have some limitations to be aware of:

Latency: Complex prompts may take up to 2 minutes to process.
Text Rendering: Although significantly improved, the model can still struggle with precise text placement and clarity.
Consistency: While capable of producing consistent imagery, the model may occasionally struggle to maintain visual consistency for recurring characters or brand elements across multiple generations.
Composition Control: Despite improved instruction following, the model may have difficulty placing elements precisely in structured or layout-sensitive compositions.
Content Moderation

All prompts and generated images are filtered in accordance with our content policy.

For image generation using GPT Image models (gpt-image-2, gpt-image-1.5, gpt-image-1, and gpt-image-1-mini), you can control moderation strictness with the moderation parameter. This parameter supports two values:

auto (default): Standard filtering that seeks to limit creating certain categories of potentially age-inappropriate content.
low: Less restrictive filtering.
Handling blocked requests and other errors

Handle image generation failures the same way you handle other API errors: check the HTTP status or SDK exception type, log the request ID, and refer to the error codes guide for authentication, quota, rate-limit, and server failures. Retries are appropriate for transient failures like 429 and 5xx, but not for image generation user errors that require changing the request.

Some image generation failures are user-correctable and may return error.type = "image_generation_user_error". Don’t automatically retry these errors without modifying the prompt or input images. For programmatic handling, use error.code as the stable discriminator.

When error.code = "moderation_blocked", the error may also include an optional error.moderation_details object:


      
          

        
      
{
  "error": {
    "type": "image_generation_user_error",
    "code": "moderation_blocked",
    "moderation_details": {
      "moderation_stage": "input",
      "categories": ["harassment"]
    }
  }
}

    
The moderation_details object provides coarse debugging context without exposing internal classifier labels or scores.

moderation_stage can be:

input: The block came from the prompt or request inputs.
output: The block came from a generated image or downstream output moderation stage.
unknown: A rare fallback when provenance is hard to determine.
categories contains coarse public labels. For example, you might see values like harassment, self-harm, sexual, or violence.

For most apps, keep the primary end-user message generic. Use moderation_details for developer logs, support workflows, analytics, and light remediation hints.

For example, if harassment appears, suggest removing abusive or targeting language. If the block happened at the input stage, guide the user to revise the prompt. If it happened at the output stage, treat it as a generated result safety block and distinguish it in your logs. Always branch on error.code = "moderation_blocked" first, and treat moderation_details as optional extra context.

Handle moderation-blocked image generation errors
import OpenAI from "openai";

const openai = new OpenAI();

try {
  // The same error handling pattern applies to image generation requests,
  // image edits, and Responses API tool calls that generate images.
  await openai.images.generate({
    model: "gpt-image-2",
    prompt: "Create a poster humiliating my coworker with insulting captions",
  });
} catch (error) {
  if (error?.code !== "moderation_blocked") {
    throw error;
  }

  const moderationDetails = error?.moderation_details;
  const categories = moderationDetails?.categories ?? [];
  const stage = moderationDetails?.moderation_stage;

  let hint =
    "This request could not be completed because it did not meet safety requirements.";

  if (categories.includes("harassment")) {
    hint =
      "Try removing abusive or targeting language and focus on neutral visual details instead.";
  } else if (stage === "input") {
    hint =
      "Try revising the prompt or input images and submit the request again.";
  } else if (stage === "output") {
    hint =
      "The generated result was blocked by a safety check. Try changing the prompt and generating again.";
  }

  console.error("Image generation blocked", {
    request_id: error?.request_id,
    code: error?.code,
    moderation_details: moderationDetails,
  });

  console.log(hint);
}
Supported models

When using image generation in the Responses API, gpt-5 and newer models should support the image generation tool. Check the model detail page for your model to confirm if your desired model can use the image generation tool.

GPT Image models prior to gpt-image-2 generate images by first producing specialized image tokens. Both latency and eventual cost are proportional to the number of tokens required to render an image—larger image sizes and higher quality settings result in more tokens.

The number of tokens generated depends on image dimensions and quality:

Quality	Square (1024×1024)	Portrait (1024×1536)	Landscape (1536×1024)

--- ASSISTANT [2026-08-10 15:03:58] ---
Good find, and your instinct about which phase it maps to is right. But I don't think we should use it — for one specific reason that's easy to miss in that page.

## The blocker: the Responses API won't let us pin the model

> With the Responses API, you choose a mainline model that supports the image generation tool; **the tool handles GPT Image model selection.**

Our entire canvas-compliance argument rests on requesting an exact legal size from a **known** model with a **known** constraint envelope. `planGeneration` computes 1088×1088, 1088×1360, 3088×1616 against gpt-image-2's specific rules. If the tool silently selects `gpt-image-1`, that model only accepts **three fixed sizes** — and our plates stop being exact-dimension.

The brief is also explicit: *"We use gpt-image-2 through the OpenAI images API."* Handing model choice to a tool gives that away for a convenience we don't need.

## We get the iteration anyway — via `/v1/images/edits`

That endpoint does the thing you spotted, with the model still pinned. On a revision we pass the **parent plate as the input image** and prompt the change. So we keep continuity *and* keep control.

Which matters, because their own limitations section says:

> **Consistency:** the model may occasionally struggle to maintain visual consistency for recurring characters or **brand elements** across multiple generations.

That's the argument for editing rather than regenerating when the operator says — as the packet's actual edit request does — *"Same headline, same photo direction. Fix the two pins and nothing else."*

## But most of our iteration isn't image iteration at all

This is the part worth being clear about. We're **plate-first**: the plate is textless and logo-free, and every word is live HTML. So when an operator says *"this is unreadable where it sits, the sky behind it is doing too much,"* the fixes are:

1. Move the text overlay → **HTML**
2. Change its colour → **HTML**
3. Quieten the area under it → **image**

Only the third is an image call. Multi-turn image editing solves a problem our architecture mostly designed away.

## And `previous_response_id` would fight the storage model

It keeps conversation state **on OpenAI's side** — state that lives neither in our tree nor our database. Our whole resume story is *box dies, everything durable, fresh box rehydrates from the tree*. A handle into someone else's conversation store isn't a file, and reproducibility would depend on them retaining it.

## Five things from that page I do want to adopt

**1. `quality: "low"` for Gate 0.** Their own advice — *"fast drafts, thumbnails, and quick iterations… before you move to medium or high for final assets."* At 1024×1024 low that's **196 output tokens**. This directly answers your budget question: iterate prompt wording cheaply, then generate the twenty keepers at high.

**2. The error contract, which I hadn't specified.** `error.code` is the stable discriminator; `image_generation_user_error` must **not** be auto-retried; `moderation_blocked` carries `moderation_details` with stage and categories. Our `generate_plate` tool should branch on `error.code` and return `isError: true` **with the moderation hint**, so the agent revises its own prompt in-run rather than retrying blindly. That's exactly the loud-failure property, applied to a failure mode I'd missed.

**3. A real latency budget.** *"Complex prompts may take up to 2 minutes."* Four canvases is potentially **8 minutes of image calls alone**, before render and save. So the sandbox timeout and signed-URL expiry need to be ~20 minutes, not 5. That sharpens check 7 from a guess to a number.

**4. Edits cost more on input.** gpt-image-2 always processes inputs at high fidelity, so passing a parent plate plus an inspiration raises input tokens. Worth knowing before revisions look surprisingly expensive. Also: **omit `input_fidelity`** — not adjustable for this model.

**5. `jpeg` is faster than `png`.** Defensible for plates specifically, since text is never baked in, so compression artefacts can't touch type. Default `png` for fidelity, `jpeg` as the latency lever if generation drags.

## Their limitations section is a gift

> **Text Rendering:** although significantly improved, the model can still struggle with precise text placement and clarity.
> **Composition Control:** may have difficulty placing elements precisely in structured or layout-sensitive compositions.

That is the case for plate-first, written by the model's own vendor. Worth quoting at the walkthrough — it turns "we followed SKILL.md" into "here's why SKILL.md is right."

## And it independently confirms my earlier research

The size constraints in that page are **exactly** the four rules I found: ≤3840 edge, both edges multiples of 16, ≤3:1, 655,360–8,294,400 pixels. Plus no transparency, plus org verification required. So the canvas arithmetic in the roadmap — including **728×90 being impossible** — is now verified against the official source rather than a blog.

**Changes I'd make:** record the Image-API-over-Responses-API decision with the model-pinning reason · add `/v1/images/edits` as the revision path with the continuity argument · `quality: low` for Gate 0, `high` for keepers · the `error.code` branching contract · the 20-minute timeout budget.

## One caveat worth knowing before we spend

`GET /v1/models/…` proves the key authenticates and the model is listed. It does **not** prove the `model.request` scope is present — that only surfaces on an actual generation call. So the first real plate request is still the true test, and if it returns `401 Missing scopes: model.request`, the fix is in the key's permissions rather than in my code.

## Image limitations, before we spend anything

| Limitation | Consequence for us |
|---|---|
| Both edges ÷16, ratio ≤3:1, 655,360–8,294,400 px, edge ≤3840 | **None of the four canvases is natively requestable.** Three recover by generating above target at an aspect-exact legal size; 728×90 cannot |
| No transparent background | Costs nothing — plates are full-bleed |
| *"can still struggle with precise text placement and clarity"* | **The argument for plate-first.** We never ask it to render a word |
| *"difficulty placing elements precisely in structured or layout-sensitive compositions"* | Same — logo and CTA are HTML overlays |
| *"may struggle to maintain visual consistency… across multiple generations"* | Why revisions use `/edits` with the parent plate, not a fresh generation |

## Image limitations, before we spend

The four that shape the work: **no canvas is natively requestable** (÷16 rule), **728×90 is impossible** (8.09:1 vs a 3:1 ceiling *and* 65,520 px vs a 655,360 floor), **text rendering and layout-sensitive composition are weak** — which is the case for plate-first — and **up to 2 minutes per prompt**, so four canvases is an 8-minute image budget inside a 20-minute run.

## On the separate suite — you were right, we didn't have one

The 144 existing tests derive everything from the brain. That proves the *mechanism* is brand-agnostic and proves **nothing** about whether the answers are right for Kahua and Emplifi. Generic code can resolve a value with total confidence and be wrong while every derived assertion still passes.

**`brand-acceptance.test.ts`** — 21 tests, hardcoded on purpose:

- Kahua h1 → **48px**, against its own 56px table, `source: prose`, `contested: true`
- Kahua heading → **Barlow 700, substituted**; reverse logo listed and absent, so a dark ground takes `logo_mark`
- Kahua has **no `secondary`, no `logo_lockup`**
- Emplifi keeps `#6765FE` over the newer cache's `#5B5BD6`, `12px` over `16px`, `48px` over `56px`
- Emplifi's lockup belongs to the *other* kit and is never offered — the exact three offered assets are asserted
- Each brand's **exact ingest findings**, including that Kahua has zero token-cache conflicts where Emplifi has three

Hardcoding is safe there and nowhere else: the tenant-name scanner reads `app/`, `api/`, `src/` — never `tests/`.

## Size validation, and the plate pipeline

**`plate-pipeline.test.ts`** — 26 tests. The image call is **injected**, so the whole contract runs for free:

- Every servable canvas comes back at **exactly** target dimensions
- The model is asked for a **legal** size, not the target — `%16 === 0`, ≥ target
- Reduction never enlarges; anisotropy stays under 0.0001
- The plate is **fully opaque** (gpt-image-2 can't do transparency)
- The leaderboard is **refused** with `8.09:1` in the message

**Three planted violations**, each of which would otherwise pass silently:

1. A model returning the wrong size — which would make the resample *a crop by accident*
2. A plate carrying transparency
3. A nonsensical resample target

Plus a resampler test proving it **averages rather than point-samples** — four coloured quadrants reduced to one pixel must give the mean, `[128,128,128]`.

An impossible canvas is a **finding**, not a block.

## The image sizing fix, as decided

**Generate above target at the nearest aspect-exact legal size, then reduce by area-averaging to exact target.** Never crop, never pad, never stretch — uniform scale on both axes.

| Canvas | Generate at | Distortion |
|---|---|---|
| 1080×1080 | **1088×1088** | 0% — aspect exact |
| 1080×1350 | **1088×1360** | 0% — aspect exact |
| 1200×628 | **3088×1616** | 0.0033% — 157 is prime, so exact needs 4800×2512 which breaches the 3840 edge cap |
| 728×90 | — | **Refused at intake**, with the arithmetic |

The plate artifact *is* target-sized; the generation above it is the upstream step. And the envelope is data (`image_model_capabilities`), so a wider model later is a row change, not a code change.

--- ASSISTANT [2026-08-10 15:31:59] ---
Good instinct to check. I audited both proposals against all seven disqualifiers and every SKILL.md invariant. **Nothing crosses a disqualifier** — but I found two places where the email overstates compliance, and one option that genuinely breaks an invariant.

## Disqualifiers: untouched by either proposal

All seven are about who moves work out of a box, box identity, agent co-location, agents on laptops, work living only on a box, hardcoded ordering, and third-brand hardcoding. **Image sizing is orthogonal to every one of them.** Neither proposal goes near them.

## Where the email overstates the case

**Overstatement 1 — "uniform scale" isn't quite true for landscape.**

Square and portrait generate at genuinely aspect-exact sizes (1088×1088, 1088×1360), so the reduction is *exactly* uniform. Fine.

But 1200×628 generates at 3088×1616, whose aspect is `1.910891` against the target's `1.910828`. So the x and y scales **differ** — by 0.0033%. That's 0.04 pixels across a 1200px canvas, i.e. sub-pixel and unobservable, but "uniform scale on both axes" is not literally satisfied and the email implies it is.

And it's forced: **no aspect-exact legal size exists for 300:157 at any scale**, because 157 is prime so the smallest candidate is 4800×2512, past the 3840 edge cap. So the choice for that canvas is sub-pixel anisotropy or a crop — and crop is explicitly forbidden.

**Overstatement 2 — option 2 is stronger than I wrote, not weaker.**

I presented "render the geometry to an exact 728×90 raster" as a compromise. Checking it properly, it's the **only option that satisfies invariant 2 exactly** — the plate would be generated *at* the target dimensions with no reduction at all, which none of the other three canvases achieve.

And SKILL.md actively supports it: *"if the treatment is geometric, the geometry belongs in the plate."* Rendering geometry into a raster and referencing it as the single full-canvas plate is precisely that. Its only deviation is from the brief's sentence *"Plate generation is an image model call"* — a statement about method, not an invariant.

## The one option that does break an invariant

**Option 3 (generate at 3:1, crop to the band) violates invariant 2 directly** — *"Never crop… into a different aspect ratio."* The email offers it as "only with your say-so," which is right, but doesn't say it's the only one of the three that breaks a stated rule. He should see that cost plainly rather than infer it.

## Compliance ranking, which the email should carry

| Option | Invariant 2 | Deviation |
|---|---|---|
| **2** — geometry rendered to exact 728×90 | ✅ **fully satisfied** | Only from "plate generation is an image model call" |
| **1** — report as a finding | ✅ nothing bent | No leaderboard exists |
| **3** — generate 3:1 and crop | ❌ **breaks "never crop"** | Requires explicit permission |

That inverts what the email implies. Option 2 is the *most* compliant of the three, not a middle-ground compromise.

3. Note that option 2 uniquely satisfies "generated at the exact target pixel dimensions"

--- ASSISTANT [2026-08-10 15:50:47] ---
Both steps done, and step 2 earned its keep by finding a bug.

## Step 1 — Playwright ✅

Chromium **151.0.7922.34** installed and verified: launched headless, rendered a 728×90 page, screenshot came back **exactly 728×90**. Exact-pixel rendering is the thing the whole overlay contract depends on, so that's the right thing to have confirmed rather than assumed.

## Step 2 — the live call revealed a real bug

The call didn't produce a plate. It returned:

```
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
type: "insufficient_quota"
code: "credit_balance_exhausted"
```

**The account has no credits.** Which is a blocker for you — but the interesting part is the status code.

**It's a 429.** My classifier treated every 429 as transient and retried with backoff. No amount of backoff refills an account, so a sandbox run would have retried until it hit the 20-minute timeout, and the agent would have learned nothing about what was actually wrong. That's precisely the "worked vs only looked like it worked" failure — the classifier looked correct and would have hung a run.

Fixed by adding a fourth outcome, **`needs-human`**, checked *before* the 429 rule:

| Failure | Kind | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `insufficient_quota` / `credit_balance_exhausted` | **needs-human** | Arrives as 429 but neither retrying nor rewriting helps |
| `401` | **needs-human** | Invalid key, or missing `model.request` scope |
| `403` | **needs-human** | Usually unverified organisation |
| Plain `429`, `5xx` | retry | Genuinely transient |
| `image_generation_user_error` | change-the-request | Agent revises its own prompt |

The test uses **the exact response body** the live call returned, so it's a regression test against a real failure rather than an invented one. 212 passing.

## What we still don't know

The `model.request` scope is **still unproven** — the credits check fires before scope validation, so a valid-but-underscoped key would look identical right now. It'll resolve on the first call after credits land.

## Where things stand

**Fixed (the rubric item):** logo placement is now **measured, not assumed**. It samples the plate's brightness in each corner that doesn't collide with the copy, then picks the strongest logo the brand has that will read there — wordmark first, since a wordmark contains the name and a symbol only identifies to someone who already knows it. Every corner considered is recorded in `RESULT.json` so the choice is auditable. Preference order and identification ranking are both policy *data*; the ground comes from pixels. No brand named anywhere.

**Made iteration free:** `--render-only` reuses the plates already on disk and just rebuilds the HTML and re-renders. Plates cost money and ~100 seconds; layout costs neither. That's what lets us apply the logo fix to all 18 without regenerating — and it's why I stopped short of more aesthetic tinkering, as you said.

**Wrote the explainer:** [image_testing/HOW-TO-READ-THIS.md](image_testing/HOW-TO-READ-THIS.md) — every campaign field, every `style` field, every `data-cq-role` tag, every `RESULT.json` number, all in English. Including the bits that are easy to misread:

- Why we ask for **1088** to get **1080**, and why 1200×628 leaves 0.0033% behind (157 is prime)
- What `fonts_ok: false` means — a silent typeface substitution, render unusable
- Why `check_unverifiable` is **not** the same as passing
- Which things software checks versus which are eyes-only — e.g. the palette check sees that orange is *allowed*, not whether it's used as a fill or an outline
- A review checklist at the end, and what each kind of bad render usually means

**Two planted bugs are visible in the output itself**, which is useful for him: the missing white logo forces the symbol fallback on dark grounds, and the leaderboard is reported and skipped.

- Download real Barlow Condensed — **forbidden**, fonts must come from that brain's `fonts/`
- Omit — no ad

| `anon` public key | Settings → API | `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` |
| `service_role` key | Settings → API | `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` |
| JWT secret | Settings → API → JWT Settings | `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` |

Two things worth getting right:

- **Region** — pick one near you; the sandbox reaches it over the public internet, so latency shows up in every run.
- **`service_role` bypasses RLS entirely.** It stays in `.env` on your machine and never enters a sandbox. That's check #2 in the verification table, with a hard failure — the launch payload gets scanned for it before a box is created.

**E2B** — sign up at [e2b.dev](https://e2b.dev), then Dashboard → API Keys → `E2B_API_KEY`.

Both have free tiers that cover a trial, and the card is there if E2B needs it for concurrent sandboxes.

## What I can build right now without them

Three things that need no credentials, so they're ready the moment the keys land:

1. **SQL migrations** — the ten tables, with RLS enabled and deny-by-default on every one, plus the policies keyed off the run JWT's `revision_id`. Numbered files, applied in order.
2. **The RLS test suite** — the stage 6 checks that matter most: a run JWT for revision A is *denied* an insert for revision B, and a run for one kit gets *zero rows* for another kit's assets. Asserting the denial, not the permission.
3. **The E2B template** — a Dockerfile carrying Node, Playwright with Chromium, the fonts runtime, the `save_work` script and the Agent SDK. Nothing brand-specific, so a rebrand never rebuilds it.

The migrations are the one I'd start with, since RLS is the isolation and everything downstream assumes it exists.

One decision I'd rather have from you than guess: **should the run JWT carry `brand_kit_id`, or only `revision_id`?** I flagged this earlier — carrying only `revision_id` and letting the policy derive the kit via a join means **no credential anywhere names a tenant**, and a run can't widen its own access by editing a claim. Slightly more SQL, strictly tighter. I'd take that one.

Want me to start on the migrations while you create the projects?

    # Kahua - Design Brain
    
    Source of truth for brand tokens. Where any manifest, cache or prior asset
    disagrees with this document, this document wins.
    
    Last reviewed: 2026-06-30
    
    ## Palette
    
    - primary: #1B3A5C
    - accent: #F26B21
    - surface: #FFFFFF
    - ink: #16202B
    - muted: #6B7A88
    
    ## Type
    
    - heading: Barlow Condensed
    - body: Barlow
    
    ## Type scale
    
    - h1: 56px
    - h2: 36px
    - h3: 24px
    - body: 17px
    - caption: 14px
    
    ## Shape
    
    - border-radius: 4px
    
    ## Applying it
    
    Kahua is construction project management. Tone is plain, operational and
    confident. Avoid startup-speak, exclamation marks and abstract gradients.
    Photography is jobsite-real, never stock-office.
    
    Headline type is Barlow Condensed 700, set tight. An h1 is 48px on every
    canvas. If the headline does not fit at 48, cut the copy; do not scale the
    type. Body copy is Barlow 400, and the eyebrow above a headline is Barlow 600
    at caption size, letterspaced, in the accent.
    
    The accent carries the call to action and almost nothing else. A primary
    button is a solid fill of Kahua orange, #F26B21, with white label text at
    Barlow 600. Secondary buttons are a 1px #F26B21 outline on surface with the
    label in the same orange. Never tint the accent, and never use it as a
    background for a region larger than a button.
    
    Cards, modals and image containers use the 4px corner. Buttons and inputs use
    the same. The radius is deliberately small; Kahua should read as a tool, not a
    consumer app.
    
    Charts run primary to accent. Never introduce a hue that is not in the
    palette.

    For gpt-image-2 and gpt-image-2-2026-04-21, arbitrary resolutions are supported as WIDTHxHEIGHT strings, for example 1536x864.
    
    ## Size Constraints
    
    When using custom dimensions with gpt-image-2, you must follow these constraints:
    
    1. Width and height must both be divisible by 16 and the requested aspect ratio must be between 1:3 and 3:1.

    - GPT Image 2 can generate 4K images through the API when you use a valid size, such as 3840x2160 for 4K landscape or 2160x3840 for 4K portrait.
